title: Reply in Five Minutes or Lose the Lead
seoTitle: Reply in Five Minutes or Lose the Lead
excerpt: A customer messaging four shops at once books with whoever replies first. Here is what five minutes versus five hours does to your bookings, and how a two-person team keeps up.
seoDescription: Why the business that replies to a WhatsApp enquiry within five minutes wins the booking, and how small Omani teams answer fast without living on the phone.

sources.label: Harvard Business Review: The Short Life of Online Sales Leads

blocks.text: A customer messages four boutiques in Al Mouj at the same time, asking about the same dress in four colours. Whoever replies first usually gets the sale, and the other three shops never even find out they lost it. Five minutes is often the whole difference between a booking and a message that just sits there unread.

segments.text: looked at how 2,241 US companies handled a new sales enquiry that arrived through their own website. Businesses that replied within an hour were close to seven times more likely to have a useful conversation with that lead than one that waited a full day. Almost a quarter of the companies in the study never replied at all.

That study was about web forms filled in years ago in another country, but the pattern behind it has nothing to do with the country or the form. Interest cools fast. A customer who messages your boutique, restaurant or clinic is warm in the first few minutes, curious in the first hour, and often gone by evening, whether the message arrived on the website, WhatsApp or an Instagram comment.

blocks.text: Why the fastest reply wins, not the best one

segments.text: Someone looking for a room in Salalah during khareef, a haircut before a wedding, or a school uniform before term starts rarely messages one business and waits. They message three or four at once, on WhatsApp, and book with whichever one answers first with a clear price and a next step, even if it costs a rial or two more elsewhere.

This is uncomfortable to admit, but it explains a lot of business that gets lost without ever looking like a complaint. The customer does not call back to say you were too slow. She books somewhere else and moves on, and you never learn the enquiry existed at all.

blocks.text: The business that answers first usually wins the customer, not the business with the better price.
What actually eats your five minutes

segments.text: None of this is about being careless. Small teams lose the five minutes to ordinary things that happen all day.

items.text: One phone and one person, with a customer already standing at the till
Driving between two branches, the bank and the supplier, all in the same afternoon
The quiet midday stretch in summer, when field staff are off the road and messages back up until the afternoon
Enquiries that land well after midnight, the same pattern behind many
, when nobody is awake to answer
Four separate inboxes on one phone: WhatsApp, Instagram, the website chat and missed calls, each needing its own reply

blocks.text: Getting there without living on your phone

segments.text: None of this means answering every message yourself at 2am. It means making sure something always answers, even when you cannot.

items.text: Turn on WhatsApp Business's greeting message and quick replies, so the first line goes out the moment a message lands, before anyone has to type
Agree who owns the phone each shift, with a clear handover time, so no enquiry sits in the gap between two people
Keep three ready answers pasted somewhere close: price, availability and location, so the human part of the reply takes seconds, not minutes

blocks.quote: If I don't reply inside a few minutes, she has already booked with someone else and forgotten she even messaged me.

segments.text: Check your own reply time before you change anything else. Open WhatsApp Business, look at how long messages sat unanswered this week, and be honest about it. If your average is measured in hours, that is the leak, not your prices, your product or your staff's manners.

blocks.title: Try this today
paragraphs: Open WhatsApp Business and check how long your last ten messages took to get a first reply.
Turn on the away message and quick replies if they are not already on.
Agree with your team, in writing, who answers between 1pm and 4pm, and after 9pm.
Pick one enquiry from today that took over an hour to answer, and ask why.

items.q: Does this apply to Instagram DMs too?
items.a: Yes. The same short shelf life applies to a comment or a DM left unanswered for hours; the customer usually books with whoever replied faster elsewhere.

items.q: Is a fast reply enough on its own?
items.a: No. Speed earns you the conversation. The reply still needs to be accurate and end in a clear next step, like a price, a slot or a booking link.

items.q: What if we genuinely cannot answer at night?
items.a: That is exactly the gap automated coverage is built for, so the enquiry is captured and waiting when a person can follow up properly in the morning.

segments.text: Speed does not replace a good product or a fair price, but it decides who even gets to compete on those. Check your reply times this week, fix the gaps you can staff, and cover the ones you cannot, and the lead that used to disappear starts turning into a booking instead.
